spatial_claims.claim: Produce a straight line and cut off successive copies of r to obtain lengths 2r and 3r
Construct mean proportional a between r and 3r, yielding a^2 = 3r^2
Construct mean proportional b between r and 2r, yielding b^2 = 2r^2
Place segments a and b consecutively on one straight line to form L

configuration_map: The proof constructs: (1) r, the assigned rational straight line; (2) lengths 2r and 3r on a line; (3) a, the mean proportional between r and 3r, so a^2 = 3r^2; (4) b, the mean proportional between r and 2r, so b^2 = 2r^2; (5) L = a + b, formed by placing a and b end-to-end. No points are placed inside or outside any figure. No angles are constructed or decomposed. No circles or triangles are involved. The entire argument is algebraic: computing squares, checking number-theoretic properties of ratios (6:2, 4:2, 3:2 are not ratios of square numbers), establishing commensurability relations, and classifying L according to Definition 10.2.6.
pass_reason: The proof is fundamentally algebraic and number-theoretic, dealing with commensurability classification of binomial lines. Its only geometric content is standard constructions (mean proportionals via 6.13, placing segments end-to-end). There are no competing spatial claims about point positions, ray orderings, angle decompositions, or inside/outside relationships. All spatial claims are trivially consistent.
